sessions.title: Evaluations with Phoenix 101
sessions.description:
You shipped an AI agent. It works great on your test queries. But how do you know it works on your users' queries? How do you know a prompt change that fixes one thing didn't break three others? And when a new model drops next quarter, how do you know whether to upgrade? If your answer to any of these is "I run it a few times and check," this workshop is for you.

In this hands-on session, you'll build a complete evaluation pipeline for an AI agent from scratch. Starting with a financial analysis chatbot built on the Claude Agent SDK, you'll instrument it with tracing, run it against diverse test cases, and then do the thing most tutorials skip: actually read your data. You'll categorize failures by root cause, define success criteria, and use that analysis to decide what to measure before writing a single eval. Then you'll build three types of evaluators: fast deterministic code checks, built-in LLM-as-a-judge evals like faithfulness, and a custom rubric you design yourself. You'll validate your judges against your own human labels, because an eval you haven't tested is just a fancy way of being wrong at scale.

The workshop doesn't stop at scoring. You'll save failure cases as reusable datasets, improve your agent's prompts based on what the evals told you, and run controlled experiments to prove the improvement with numbers instead of gut feel. Along the way, you'll learn practical frameworks: the impact hierarchy for prioritizing fixes, the Swiss Cheese model for layering defenses, and the eval-iterate cycle that turns a prototype into a production system. You'll leave with a working notebook, a free Phoenix Cloud account with your traces and eval results, and a repeatable process you can apply to any AI application the day you get home.

sessions.title: AI Evaluation 101
sessions.description: Building an AI demo is easy. Knowing whether it actually works — and keeping it working in production — is the hard part. Most teams ship agents on vibes: they try a few prompts, the output looks good, and they push to production with no real way to measure quality or catch regressions. This hands-on workshop walks through the full lifecycle of shipping a real AI agent, using a working financial-analyst agent built on the Claude Agent SDK as the running example. You'll instrument it with tracing, do structured error analysis on its actual outputs, and build a layered evaluation suite — from cheap deterministic code checks to LLM-as-a-judge evaluators with custom rubrics. We'll cover the parts most tutorials skip: why agents fail in ways single LLM calls don't, the eval anti-patterns that quietly mislead you, and how to know whether you can even trust your judge (meta-evaluation). Finally, we'll close the loop: turning eval results into datasets and experiments, running evals online against production traffic, wiring them to monitors and alerts, and feeding failure explanations back to a coding agent to actually fix the underlying problems. You'll leave with a runnable notebook and a repeatable, evaluation-driven workflow you can apply to your own agents the next day.

sessions.title: Harbor Intro: Shipping agents on evidence, not vibes
sessions.description: Harbor is an open-source framework for evaluating agents on realistic tasks with real data in isolated, sandboxed environments. This talk gives a conceptual overview of how Harbor works: tasks defined as natural-language instructions, agents run in fresh Docker environments, verifiers that grade what the agent leaves behind, and rewards that close the loop so you can change a prompt, tool, skill, or whole architecture and get immediate feedback. We’ll see how Harbor integrates with Phoenix, an open-source AI observability, experimentation, and evaluation platform, and discuss concrete examples of how the Phoenix team is using Harbor to iterate more quickly and with greater confidence. You'll leave with a working mental model of Harbor and a sense of how to apply it to your own agents.

sessions.title: Agent = Model + Harness: Build your own Memory-Aware AML AI Agent Harness for Financial Crime Detection
sessions.description:
Agent = Model + Harness. The model emits tokens; state, memory, retrieval, tool dispatch, identity, retries, and budgets. All these concepts are harness code — and that is where agent quality is won or lost.

In this hands-on workshop, you build that harness from primitives against Oracle AI Database and a realistic AML dataset: Meridian Bank, 25 branches, ~1,200 transactions over 90 days, and transactions flagged by Anti Money Laundering (AML) rules.

We will go through long-term memory and schema scanning with OAMP, semantic and hybrid RRF retrieval with ONNX in-database embeddings, vector-indexed toolbox and skillboxes, and a bounded agent_turn loop.

After this workshop, you will know everything required to build your own agent harness from scratch, staying faithful to best agent harness and AI practices.

You leave with a readable ~100-line loop you can operate, and a mental model that you can improve for your financial AI agents.

sessions.title: Agents that Self Improve While You Sleep
sessions.description:

Arize's Signal agent reviews them and files what it finds the way a reviewer would. From there a failure becomes a dataset, the finding becomes an eval, and that eval becomes the regression test guarding the fix. The pieces are tracing, Signal, datasets, evaluators and experiments. The workshop is about how they connect.

What you'll learn:

• How to turn a production failures into a permanent tests

• How to write an eval from a problem the system found instead of guessing at criteria up front

• How to validate fixes without regressing something else

• Where to add humans to the loop

sessions.title: Beyond “Done”: Building Verification Loops for AI Agents
sessions.description:
Delegating work takes more than a capable model and a good prompt. It takes a system that can check results, catch unsupported claims, and decide when to retry or ask for help.

In this hands-on, 60-minute workshop, you’ll build a verification and repair loop around an AI agent. We’ll use Playwright to check browser behavior and Jev to evaluate whether collected evidence supports specific acceptance criteria. Your code will combine those signals to accept work, request a bounded repair, or escalate to a human.

Then we’ll try to fool it. Using deliberately broken outputs and misleading evidence, you’ll test not just the agent, but the verifier itself, and explore the trade-off between catching failures and interrupting people unnecessarily.

Drawing on real projects involving delegated work and agent supervision, this workshop focuses on patterns you can apply with your own stack. You’ll leave with a working verification loop and a practical method for deciding what to automate, what to check, and where human judgment still belongs.

You need to give the model enough data to make predictions without accidentally giving it access to up-to-date information about the events it’s trying to predict. On top of that, if your model has any access to search, it’s hard to prevent or detect cheating. Ideally, the agent should simply be able to search  the web as it was on any given date in the past.

Now it can. Exa Snapshot is a research preview built on more than 400 billion webpage snapshots from the last two decades. In this session, Ryan Ahern (Forward Deployed Engineer at Exa) will show you how Exa Snapshot can be used to backtest prediction agents against yesterday’s web. The session suits both AI leaders and engineers. Bring a laptop if you want to follow along: a seed script loads the demo into your own Langfuse project.

Vault: Making Unstructured Data Work for Investing
sessions.description:
Model intelligence and persistence have reached a level where we believe applied AI in the enterprise is now about context and connectors. Out of the box frontier intelligence in the investment domain is fundamentally limited by access to information.
Bridgewater's investment philosophy is fundamental and systematic. We work to uncover truths about how economies operate, building up that understanding on one of the world's most comprehensive bitemporal structured data stores. But our investors don't work from structured data alone. They consume research, news, transcripts, and internal writing every day. An agent tasked with investment problems needs access to the same information our best human investors have, so we built the Vault: a centralized, high-quality repository of our best external and internal unstructured data, serving humans and agents alike.
We'll walk through why we chose to solve this problem ourselves, tracing the Vault from our first instinct, which was to buy it, through expanding it across all of our third-party research and into our internal knowledge, building it up from a point solution into a platform. The Vault already powers PAT, our first generation of analyst agents, used daily by hundreds of Bridgewater investors, and is now enabling our second-generation Researcher.

sessions.title: Balancing Acceleration and Safety for AI Agents

In this talk, I’ll cover some of the key technical approaches we use and have found highly effective at Two Sigma, and along the way hopefully convince you that there doesn’t need to be a tradeoff between these two properties.

sessions.title: Does Code Quality Even Matter?
sessions.description: There's so much debate online about "should we read the code?" Some people are yelling, "Everybody should build everything with a dark factory!" sessions.title: What does an AI engineer do?
sessions.description: Coding agents have effectively eliminated the need for manually writing code, and the current frontier is how to eliminate code review. But where are we going if we look past that? What happens when agents master devops, architecture, scaling, and security? What is an engineer if agents can do all the building? In this look into the next few years, Aparna Dhinakaran argues that the core skill that remains is the definition of “good”: knowing what your users want, and what it looks like when it’s “done”, are the two things agents don’t know and aren’t going to get to. At the same time, more and more AI is going to be involved in software, so software is going to get steadily less deterministic. That presents a dual challenge: you have to get good at defining success, while simultaneously success gets harder to measure. How to tackle those challenges is the subject of this talk.

Turning AI Into Operating Margin: A Field Report from Private Equity
sessions.description:
Private equity firms hold controlling stakes in companies across nearly every sector - cargo airlines, education publishers, insurance brokers, industrial manufacturers. That makes PE one of the largest and least discussed deployment surfaces for AI: one operating team, dozens of companies, and a hard requirement that results show up in the P&L before the company is sold. This talk covers how that actually works.
Drawing on portfolio operations work at a large PE firm, I'll walk through:

Diligence: how AI risk and opportunity get assessed before a deal closes, and how AI assumptions now enter the underwriting model itself
Deployment: what generalizes across a portfolio and what doesn't, with case studies in air cargo network decisioning and AI-native education products
Build vs. partner: which capabilities a firm builds centrally as reusable IP, and where it stays model-agnostic across vendors
Measurement: how AI work gets tied to operating margin, and what happens to projects that can't show it

Portfolio companies rarely look like a research lab: thin engineering teams, fragmented data, and a three-to-five-year clock. This is a report on shipping AI under those constraints.

sessions.title: Wells Fargo Foundation Model: Application to Fraud Detection at Scale

sessions.title: Can Any Model Write Like Me? Building a Benchmark for Creative Writing
sessions.description:
Four months ago, out of frustration with slop, I set out to answer one question: which model writes a YouTube script that sounds like me. Not best in general, not best at writing. Which one passes as my voice, on my channel, by my standards, and isn't cringe to read out loud.

So I vibe coded my own benchmark to answer it.

Benchmarking 148 models took about two weeks, two 20x subscriptions on Claude and Codex, and $80 in API credits. That was never the bottleneck.

The four months went into learning to build a proper benchmark. Deciding what a score means when the thing you are measuring is taste. Writing rubrics that quantify my subjectivity. Working out whether Elo was even the right tool. Finding out the same drafts average 74 out of 100 with one judge and 88 with another. Writing 10 scripts with two human editors and withholding half, so I could tell whether a model is contaminated.

Most of the benchmark uses automated judging, but human judging is crucial for analyzing taste.

So I added human ratings, sat down, and rated the first few hundred pairwise comparisons myself. My evaluation was broken, and only doing the work by hand revealed it.

I fixed it, rated again, and I am releasing the benchmark publicly to get help rating these models.

I will show the architecture, the numbers, what it cost, and the failure modes I would look for first in yours.

sessions.title: The Intelligence Plane: What your agents know, remember and learn
sessions.description:
Every firm can buy the same frontier models. What separates one firm's agents from another's is what they know about the business, what they remember, and whether they improve. In financial services that is also where entitlements, audit and model risk sit, which is why so many agents stall between pilot and production.

Take one request: an analyst asks an agent for the firm's exposure to a counterparty. The model can write the query. What it cannot know is that the counterparty is a dozen legal entities, that two desks calculate exposure differently, that this analyst is cleared to see only one of them, and that the agent was corrected on this exact request last week. A better model fixes none of that.

Fixing it is the job of what we call the intelligence plane: a slice through the agent stack covering application, data, ontology and semantics, memory, and the governance that wraps them. I will follow that request through the plane one layer at a time, closing each gap as we go, then show how to build your own on Oracle. If that analyst asked your agent tomorrow, how many of those four things would it know?

sessions.title: Deploying AI Inside 5 Major Banks Without the 12-Month Compliance Bottleneck
sessions.description:
Getting an enterprise AI agent through a Tier-1 bank’s security review and into an air-gapped VPC typically takes 9 to 12 months, period. Standard architectures built for SaaS envs immediately break when forced into strict data sovereignty, non-deterministic risk environments, and zero-leakage requirements.

I lead the team that's done this inside 5 different Fortune 100 banks and discovered which problems are universal and which were just one bank's weird legacy system. A few things I've seen from this work: 1) An agent that writes and runs its own exploit test to prove a CVE is actually closed. 2) An LLM judge that leaks the exact PII it was supposed to protect via its own explanation (checked 11 observability platforms and only one attempts a fix). 3) And why the database most AI observability platforms run on has no managed data resilience story at all.

I'll share the architectural and leadership blueprint behind all of this:

1. Accelerating Compliance Velocity: How to automate Docker package scanning and CVE remediation pipelines so security reviews don't become a burden for eng teams

2. Zero-Leakage Architecture: Design patterns for running agent quality and governance loops without exposing PII or violating data sovereignty rules

3. High-Availability SLAs & DR: Building zero-data-loss, multi-region failover setups that pass rigorous audits

speakers.name: Al Chen
speakers.bio: Al Chen is a Software Engineering Leader at Cisco, where he leads the customer engineering team for Splunk Agent Observability (formerly Galileo). He specializes in production AI infrastructure, enterprise deployments, and agent engineering across Fortune 100 financial institutions.

sessions.title: The Automated Security Master: keeping your master database clean with agents
sessions.description: Join Amol (CEO of Nori Agentic), Cliff (CTO of Nori Agentic), and their cloud agent Jiro as they discuss how cloud agents work, why sec masters are important, and how they worked alongside a Fortune 200 asset management firm to automate their sec master maintenance.

speakers.name: Amol Kapoor
speakers.bio:
Amol is the CEO of Nori Agentic, the Lead Organizer of AgenticsNYC, and the author of 12GramsOfCarbon. He has been at the cutting edge of ML for 12 years, and spends most of his day thinking about how to get his agents to do more things for him.

Before Nori, Amol was the CTO at consumer vector databases company SOOT.com. Before that, he was at Google Research, where he studied graph learning, representation learning, and computer vision. And before that, he was studying how ML interpretability techniques could be applied to connectomics at the BioNet lab at Columbia.

speakers.name: Clifford Ressel

sessions.title: Inside Arca’s long-horizon agents that run the business
sessions.description:
What is an AI-native company? At Arca, it means a company where you can steer the business by steering the agents.

This talk gives you a look inside the agent runtime for Arca's long-horizon work: a single goal spanning weeks, crossing multiple human hands, and internal/external systems. We’ll look at our agent loop, our signals engine, tools for long-horizon work, and how we orchestrate human/AI collaboration to drive business outcomes.

sessions.title: Write the Answer First: Generating Eval Datasets for Agents With No Benchmark
sessions.description:
Not long ago, nobody knew what a good evaluation strategy for a RAG system looked like. Each team invented its own, and it took months. Then RAGAS arrived. Faithfulness, context relevance, and answer relevance became a playbook you could look up, and the same evaluation now takes a week.

What's the equivalent for a custom agent, like one that reviews contracts, triages invoices, or runs your internal workflows? Nothing. There's no benchmark, no labels, and no playbook, so every team is back to inventing its own and losing the same months.

This talk shares the techniques I used to generate eval datasets for an agent no benchmark covers, along with how to tell when a generated dataset will help you and when it will quietly mislead you. It won't be RAGAS for agents, but it will be enough to get started on Monday.

sessions.title: No Cash Left Behind: Vanguard's Ledger Modernization Journey
sessions.description: How do you migrate hundreds of thousands of daily financial transactions off a decades-old mainframe and onto a cloud-native platform — without losing a single dollar, or a single night's sleep? At Vanguard, our Cash Program team took on exactly that challenge: rebuilding the ledger system underpinning the firm's cash offerings as a resilient, active-active microservices ecosystem, migrated while the legacy system stayed live in production. The key to pulling this off was running three tracks in parallel: producer migration, gold copy replication, and consumer migration. This let producers and consumers move independently, each on their own timeline, while data stayed consistent across both systems throughout. We'll walk through each track in turn. On the producer side, we'll cover how we onboarded dozens of data sources — APIs, direct service calls, and raw table inserts — onto the new platform. For gold copy, we'll dig into how CDC-based replication jobs kept legacy and cloud data in sync, and the tradeoffs and near-misses that came with running two systems at once. On the consumer side, we'll explain how we used GraphQL to decouple cash data from security transfer data, and why that mattered for downstream teams. Along the way, we'll touch on the architecture that made this possible — including why we built idempotency directly into the database layer instead of as a bolt-on service — and how AI tools helped us maintain two codebases through a multi-year migration. You'll leave with practical takeaways for modernizing high-stakes financial infrastructure without missing a transaction.

speakers.name: Gareth Yoder
speakers.bio: Gareth is Vanguard's Cash Program Technical Lead and founding member of the Cash Plus Program.  He also drove modernization outcomes of migrating legacy ledger ecosystems to the cloud.  Gareth is passionate about solving complex problems with innovative engineering solutions.

sessions.title: Can AI Reconstruct a Company?
sessions.description:
What if LLMs could turn a company’s public data into an executable model of how the business works, instead of just another summary?

We’re building an agent that takes 10-Ks, 10-Qs, earnings calls, and other public data and reconstructs a company like NVIDIA into a model of its key business drivers. You can run scenarios like “What happens if hyperscaler AI capex drops 20%?” and see the impact across the business.

Then we time-travel the agent back to previous quarters, give it only the information available at the time, and test how well it predicts what happens next through AutoResearch. We’ll demo the system and share what we learned about turning unstructured data into an interactive business model you can actually run, test, and evaluate.

speakers.name: Omar El Mghari
speakers.bio:
Omar El Mghari, CPA, PMP, MBA
Finance leader · CPA · Building AI-agent-driven accounting systems

I'm a finance and accounting leader with 25+ years as a CFO, Head of Internal Audit, Finance Consultant, and CPA, with deep expertise in financial reporting, internal audit, SOX compliance and readiness, and SOC 1 & 2 engagements.

For the last six years, I've also been turning that expertise into working software — building accounting and AI-enabled applications in Next.js, Python, and Firestore, merging accounting discipline with AI efficiency. That work culminated in pmsox.io, a reconciliation and integration platform that brings e-commerce and startup systems together into one accurate, auto-reconciled ledger. I also design and build multi-agent AI systems: I coded an education platform where a network of specialized AI agents autonomously grades student work and handles the surrounding workflow in the background. I'm now applying that same agent-network framework to reconciliation — where ingestion, matching, exception handling, and journal-entry generation are natural roles for specialized, coordinated agents.

Earlier, as CFO, I modernized the finance function of a ~$1B pharmaceutical company, leading 32 accountants across five countries (seven direct reports), supported by a McKinsey team. I also built a new internal audit department from the ground up for a ~$500M construction company. My SOX and internal audit work (CIA) spans multiple industries — largely from the IT and project-management side (PMP, CISA) — across the major ERPs (SAP, PeopleSoft, Oracle, NetSuite, Dynamics, Deltek) as well as QuickBooks and Sage.

sessions.title: Search the Web as It Was: An Introduction to Exa Snapshot
sessions.description: Quant teams rely on point-in-time data for prices and fundamentals, but there has never been a point-in-time view of the whole web. At least until now. Exa Snapshot lets you search and retrieve the web as it existed on any date, using more than 400 billion page snapshots from the past 20 years. We'll walk through three uses: backtesting signals drawn from the web, keeping answer leakage out of agent evals, and reconstructing what was public at a specific moment for underwriting and KYB/KYC. You'll leave knowing how to try it with `snapshotAsOf` and how to talk to us about full coverage.

sessions.title: Intent Based Auth
sessions.description:
“Is this tool call allowed?” It’s never that simple.

Allowing or denying individual API calls or MCP tools isn’t enough. You might give an agent access to read-only Notion MCP tools, for example, but still have no way to limit it to a specific database on a specific page.

Intent-based auth adds the missing context: what is this agent trying to accomplish, and does this action serve that mission?

We'll explore how AAuth, a new protocol designed for agents, allows you to track an agent's mission, how intent is enforced, and why intent based auth is key to unlocking agentic commerce.

speakers.name: Ian Livingstone
speakers.bio: Ian Livingstone is the Co-Founder & CEO of Keycard, the identity and access platform for AI agents. A three-time founder, prolific angel investor, and massive infrastructure nerd, Ian has spent 15+ years building developer tools and security infrastructure and is now focused on identity, authorization, and access control for autonomous software. Previously, he shaped platform strategy at Snyk and held senior engineering roles at Salesforce. He co-hosts The Infra Pod, covering the technical and economic shifts reshaping how software gets built and run.

speakers.name: Michael Davis
speakers.bio: Michael A. sessions.title: Your Financial Agent Passed Every Eval. Can You Defend Its Decision?
sessions.description:
A financial agent can pass every eval and still produce a decision no one can defend. The citation may point to the wrong document. The reasoning may omit the key business rule. The benchmark may treat last year's policy as today's ground truth. A high aggregate score can hide the failure that matters most.

Defensibility requires four distinct controls: authorization, execution control, evidence provenance, and evaluation integrity. Using a synthetic audit decision trace, I'll work through each control: limiting what an agent can do, preserving what it did so contested steps can be reproduced, binding its material claims to the correct sources, and verifying whether its benchmark can be trusted. I'll also show where the agent should stop and a human should decide.

You'll leave with a practical assurance pattern for financial agents whose decisions may be challenged months or years later. When that challenge comes, "the model said so" is not a defensible answer.

speakers.name: Anirudh Veeraragavan
speakers.bio: Anirudh is Lead Security Engineer and the founding security hire at Fieldguide, the leading transformation partner for agentic audit and advisory. Previously, he spent five years at Plaid, most recently as a Staff Software Security Engineer, where he led product security initiatives, including a workstream focused on developing agentic penetration-testing systems.

sessions.title: Building Agentic PDLC Systems that Scale
sessions.description:
Key themes:

• What are the key shifts in organizations that get AI/Agentic PDLC right?

• How to manage skills/agents proliferation, without slowing innovation?

• How to ensure and drive quality in agentic PDLC?

• With coding activity compressed, where do we see bottlenecks form up in the PDLC?

• What metrics/outcomes can organizations use to measure effectiveness of agentic PDLC?

sessions.title: The best context isn't in your database. It's in the investor's head.
sessions.description: In finance, the data that moves a decision rarely lives in a feed or a database. It lives in the investor's head: the position they carry, the risk they're worried about, the mandate they answer to. That's as true for an asset manager or a hedge fund PM as it is for a trader. LLMs are only as good as the context you give them, and that context is tacit, different for every person, and changes by the hour, so a generic tool hands everyone the same mediocre answer on stale data. This talk reframes the real problem in enterprise AI for finance as context engineering: not a bigger model, but capturing each user's evolving mental model and spending every token on what only they care about, without their data ever leaving the firm. I'll walk through how we think about per-user context, memory, and grounding for agents on live markets, and the security posture that lets any of this clear a bank. And I'll leave you with the open question I think decides who wins enterprise AI in finance: if the real edge lives in people's heads, how much of it can a machine actually capture?

speakers.name: Anekha Sokhal
speakers.bio: Anekha Sokhal traded derivatives at J.P. Morgan for nearly a decade. sessions.title: Can Your AI Analyst Keep a Secret?
sessions.description:
To be useful, an AI agent must be able to search *all* the data its user can access—and none they can’t. This is straightforward when the corpus is small. On millions of documents with overlapping and frequently changing permission scopes, it becomes a serious systems problem that prevents many enterprise agents from reaching prod.

Bridgewater had to solve this problem while building the Vault, a centralized, high-quality repository containing millions of unstructured documents, including confidential data governed by user-level permissions. The Vault underpins several agents, including PAT, Bridgewater’s AI Analyst. PAT is already in production and is used daily by hundreds of Bridgewater investors.

We'll trace why permission models that work at small scale, such as prefiltering on allowlists, don’t work as the corpus grows in size and complexity. Then we’ll show how Bridgewater and turbopuffer enforce complex row-level permissions at the retrieval layer rather than the app layer.

*this is a co-presentation between Bridgewater and turbopuffer*

sessions.title: Lies, Damned Lies, and Evals: How to trust your agents when the stakes are high
sessions.description:
Your coding agent scores 74%. The release decision is due today. Nobody can say what that number has earned the right to decide.

That ambiguity matters everywhere, but especially in regulated industries. Agents can modify transaction systems, access controls, reporting pipelines, and compliance-sensitive infrastructure. When software can affect money, customers, or regulatory obligations, “the benchmark looked good” is not a defensible release argument. Trust has to be supported by evidence that can survive challenge.

An eval score compresses a model, task set, execution environment, evaluator, grader, and one sample from a variable process into a single number. Financial institutions have spent decades developing disciplines for decisions built on imperfect models: define the intended use, validate performance, expose limitations, independently challenge assumptions, and monitor what happens in production. In AI, we often just print the result to one decimal place and put it on a leaderboard.

In this talk, I’ll put one convincing score on trial. The audience will choose between two release candidates, then reconsider that decision as I reveal what the aggregate concealed: a +5.4-point win in my own repository-level eval that shrank to +0.35 after repeated runs; a widely cited coding benchmark whose sponsor stopped reporting it after uncovering flawed tasks and contamination; and model graders that agreed with one another while missing the defects the release gate was supposed to catch.

We’ll rebuild the decision around five checks:

- What decision is this score allowed to change?

- How large is the run-to-run variance?

- Does the task distribution match the real workload?

- Which plausible failures can the evaluator actually detect?

- What are the grader’s true-positive and false-positive rates at the chosen threshold?

You’ll leave with a practical evidence standard for deciding when an agent has earned greater autonomy, and when a precise score is disguising uncertainty that still belongs with a human decision-maker.

speakers.name: Stephanie Jarmak

sessions.title: Inside the Fable War Room
sessions.description: "Inside the Fable War Room" is the story of an enterprise experiment we ran in collaboration with Anthropic to aggressively forward-deploy their latest Fable model into some of our most complex distributed legacy systems. Rather than handing engineers another coding assistant, we put a small cross-functional team in a room, surrounded them with a network of on-call technical, product, and business experts, and armed Fable with a clear modernization strategy, a serious compute budget, access to the relevant tools and context, and a carefully-curated playbook. This playbook consisted of rules, skills, insider system archaeology and validation tips, instructions for Fable to continuously route questions back to the humans who could answer them in the form of editable Figma diagrams and interactive worksheets. We packaged the approach as an adaptable plugin methodology that other teams at GEICO can tailor to their own systems and architecture. On it's first day, this this approach saved the company $275k/year.

speakers.name: Ford Prior

sessions.description:

Beyond the technical architecture of our MCP gateway and Agent Orchestration System, we'll focus on the foundations that make it possible to scaling an agent to hundreds of technical and non-technical staff.

You will learn how we drove widespread adoption by integrating directly into Slack, how we balanced model non-determinism with the rigid guardrails required to keep our data secure, and the secret sauce of LLMs* that powers it all.

sessions.title: Lunch Break
Networking Break
Agents can pay. So why don’t they?
sessions.description:
The payment rails for agents are now readily available, but almost nobody uses them. The problem is not simply that people do not trust agents with money. It is that the basic one-shot payment flow handles only the easiest kind of purchase.

x402’s `exact` scheme and MPP’s `charge` intent require a fixed price before execution begins, which only covers simple API calls. Newer primitives like x402’s `upto` and `batch-settlement` schemes and MPP’s `session` intent support variable or incremental charging, but they do not by themselves solve the full lifecycle of a job that runs for six hours and costs whatever it costs.

I run a marketplace of 50,000+ community-built web data and automation tools, where all three purchase types occur in production. Fixed-price calls were easy to add. Metered usage took months to implement and still requires our own metering and orchestration layer. We still have not solved long-running jobs end to end, and I don’t think anyone has.

I’ll explain where each protocol broke down in practice, what our transaction data reveals about where agent buyers actually stall, and the three things a complete agent-purchase stack still needs beyond the payment specs: a standard lifecycle for long-running jobs, auditable metering and delivery, and post-settlement refunds and recourse.

sessions.title: 1,368 AI Failures: What They Teach Us About System Evals
sessions.description:
We analyzed 1,368 documented AI failures across healthcare, financial services, law enforcement, professional services, and consumer technology.

The clearest lesson was not simply that AI models fail.

AI risk lives in the system, not just the model.

In our analysis, 92% of incidents implicated multiple weaknesses simultaneously. The typical documented failure crossed several parts of the deployed system: technical behavior, data, workflows, human oversight, controls, exposure, and downstream consequence.

That creates a fundamental problem for how we evaluate increasingly agentic AI systems.

Most evals still ask some version of one question:

Did the model or agent complete the task correctly?

But task success is not system success.

An agent can reach the expected answer after retrieving unsupported evidence, selecting the wrong tool, passing invalid arguments, crossing an authority boundary, or taking an action that should never have been available to it.

The output can say “pass” while the system tells a different story.

Drawing on the research behind our forthcoming book, Evaluable AI: From Model Evals to System Evals, this talk introduces a different unit of evaluation: the deployed AI system.

We use Risk-Based Evaluability Design (R-BED) to organize system evaluation around three connected questions:

Technical Failure: Where can the system fail?

Deployment Harm: Under what conditions can that failure reach people, processes, or consequential decisions?

Business Impact: If it does, how broadly and severely can the consequence propagate, and what can be recovered?

These questions cannot be collapsed into a single score or task-success metric. A technically weak system may remain contained. A seemingly small technical error may become material because authority, exposure, or controls allow it to propagate. And a system that appears to perform well may still be difficult to trust if its behavior cannot be reconstructed and challenged.

This leads to the concept at the center of the talk: evaluability.

Evaluability is the ability to determine, with evidence, whether a deployed AI system remains within acceptable bounds and continues to serve its intended purpose.

For agentic systems, that means making the trajectory observable: the evidence retrieved, sources used, tool selected, arguments passed, state transitions made, authority exercised, human interventions triggered, and actions taken.

Tanmay Sah and I will demonstrate this through a reproducible evaluation pipeline applied to benchmark agent trajectories. We will show where task-level success can conceal failures elsewhere in the trajectory, what can be evaluated directly from system evidence, where an evaluator or judge is required, and when the correct evaluation result is not pass or fail but insufficient evidence.

We then turn those findings into an engineering discipline:

BUILD: Define the system claim, operating boundary, evidence requirements, and permitted authority.

BREAK: Stress the system, discover failure regions, and trace failures across evidence, execution, tools, workflows, and controls.

FIX: Constrain, redesign, route, monitor, or intervene, then verify that the change actually worked.

The key insight is that meaningful system evals cannot simply be bolted onto an AI application after it has been built.

If the system does not expose the evidence needed to reconstruct what happened, important questions become impossible to answer.

Evaluability has to be designed into the system.

As AI systems become more autonomous and gain access to tools, workflows, data, and consequential actions, the distance between a technical error and a real-world consequence is shrinking.

The next generation of evals therefore cannot stop at asking:

“Did the model get the answer right?”

They must also ask:

Where can the system fail? Can that failure reach the real world? What happens if it does, and did we build enough evidence into the system to know?

speakers.name: Vishal Srivastava
speakers.bio:
Vishal Srivastava, PhD, works at the intersection of AI evaluation, model risk, and production governance for high-stakes AI systems in financial services. His work focuses on a central challenge in modern AI engineering: how to build generative and agentic systems whose evidence, behavior, and downstream consequences can be traced, tested, and challenged in production.

He develops methods for system-level AI evaluation, consequence-aware testing, evidence quality, and evaluability. His work includes Risk-Based Evaluability Design (R-BED), a framework for connecting technical failure, deployment harm, and business impact, as well as a three-layer approach to evaluating AI systems across evidential integrity, execution integrity, and deployment consequence.

He is the author of the forthcoming book Evaluable AI: From Model Evals to System Evals.

speakers.name: Tanmay Sah
speakers.bio: Tanmay Sah is a quantitative modeling and AI practitioner with more than 14 years of industry experience. His work focuses on agentic AI systems, world models, AI verification, and model validation. He is the creator of TanML, an open-source toolkit for automated model development and validation, and has conducted research on the safety and reliability of tool-using AI agents. Tanmay has presented his work at ACM conferences and the AI Engineer World’s Fair and holds a PhD in Data Science.

sessions.title: Your Next User Is an Agent
sessions.description: Your next user may be an agent discovering your API, creating an account, and taking action on someone’s behalf. Drawing on lessons from building for agents from registration to revocation, we’ll explore how onboarding, identity, and authorization change when agents become your users.

speakers.name: Isabelle Williams
speakers.bio: Isabelle Williams is a Product Manager at WorkOS focused on agent identity. Her work draws on experience across identity providers, service providers, and the infrastructure that connects enterprise identity across both. Previously, she led MongoDB’s IAM platform and launched its OAuth authorization server, powering app and agent access to MongoDB’s API and MCP server. Before MongoDB, she worked on enterprise identity governance at Microsoft Entra ID.

sessions.title: Buy, Then Deploy: Using M&A to Drive AI Transformation
sessions.description:
The next great AI companies may already exist, but they may not look like ones yet. Many businesses in mission-critical industries have entrenched customer relationships and strong market presence, but they lack the know-how to integrate AI and drive outcomes.

M&A of traditional services businesses is one strategy for closing that gap. But how do you decide which industries to focus on? What makes a good AGI-proof business? And how do you deploy AI into those companies with measurable financial impact?

This talk highlights learnings from bringing AI into the real world, what works and what doesn't, and how to evaluate opportunities for AI transformation. We present a different way to think about M&A: not as a financial engineering tactic, but as the go-to-market strategy for AI deployment.

sessions.title: From RAG to Memory: Building Agents That Remember
sessions.description: RAG is about four lines of code, and it works fine until the conversation gets interesting. Then your agent forgets what you said two turns ago and starts repeating itself, while the token bill climbs. This talk is about the jump from retrieval to memory: why a read path stops being enough, and what you build in its place. We'll separate the kinds of memory worth keeping apart, then reassemble the prompt every turn instead of letting it grow forever. You'll leave knowing why the memory layer is the part of your stack nobody else can copy.

speakers.name: Wojciech Pluta
speakers.role: Director of AI Technical Product Marketing

sessions.title: Proving Alpha: Showcasing AI's Value in Fundamental Investing
sessions.description:
Every investment firm should have AI in their budget. However, far fewer can say what it returned, especially when it comes to a traditional, fundamental equity investing strategy. We are going to showcase the methods we've built to prove how agent workflows measurably contribute to performance when returns are made up of so many different factors.

In a long/short hedge fund, the AI workflows we've developed sit directly in the investment process, rather than alongside it. Collaborating with our investors & researchers to develop tooling together has led to high-value products that get used daily, including those for new idea generation, overnight news synthesis, and earnings preview. These workflows greatly improve the research process, and we are now able to trace their impact back to the book.

We'll discuss how every idea that a workflow produces is logged at the moment of generation, along with its source and reasoning, so it can be scored for utility. From there, we have built systems to track how many ideas reach our PM to become positions, and how those positions perform against given benchmarks. For softer AI-native signals, we grade against the traditional way that same metric would have been produced and measure both time & signal improvements. This has made great strides to solve one of the biggest challenges in AI implementation: understanding the ROI and alpha generated by every tool and decision made via these systems.

We'll walk through this measurement and attribution process, both from a technical lens as well as a product framework. Ranging from the successes to pitfalls, this talk will have you energized and prepared to start measuring the impact of AI in your investment decisions.

speakers.name: Hari Kumar
speakers.role: Head of AI and Data Science
speakers.bio: Hari Kumar joined Contour Asset Management as their Head of AI. He leads the development of internal AI systems to improve the scope and efficiency of their fundamental investing strategy. Before joining Contour, he worked at Meta, where he was a member of the data science team focusing on recommendation algorithms & growth prediction. Prior to that, he worked at Boston Consulting Group in their technical enablement pillar. Mr. Kumar received an M.S.E in Computer Science and a B.S. in Finance from the University of Pennsylvania.

sessions.title: Factories of Loving Grace
sessions.description:
If you care about someone, you should build them a factory.

I built one to help my colleagues publish what they know, and another to turn my family’s days into illustrated storybooks. Through real requests, revisions, and finished work, I’ll show how AI can improve narrative outcomes when human intention, craft, and judgment shape the process.

Years of making something teach you what good looks like. That knowledge can become a tool other people use to tell stories you couldn’t tell for them. This talk is about building that capability, putting it in their hands, and finding your own contentment in what they make.

sessions.title: How frontier AI changes tolerable risk for open source security in financial services
sessions.description:
For decades, financial institutions have managed open source software risk by accepting it. Legacy applications, strict change control, and the operational risk of touching business-critical systems made a growing CVE backlog the cost of doing business.

That calculation no longer holds. Frontier models can now surface dormant vulnerabilities and chain weaknesses across the open source software supply chain faster than traditional security processes can investigate and patch them, while regulators, auditors, and customers demand stronger evidence of software integrity.

Join us to explore how financial institutions can rethink how they govern and adopt open source as risks accelerate. We’ll discuss why reactive vulnerability management is breaking down, and how teams can reduce risk without disrupting business-critical systems, and the practices security and platform leaders can use to establish a more secure, governed approach to open source consumption.

sessions.title: Coffee Break - Expo Floor
Evals in 5 minutes
sessions.description: What's an eval? Why are they important? How does Arize help you do them? Head on over to the Arize AI booth to get the lightning version of our introduction to the art and science of evals.

sessions.description: Why Modal Is Built for AI Agents at Scale

sessions.title: Can AI Understand a Distressed Credit?
sessions.description:
Distressed credit and restructuring is one of the most specialized areas of finance. The data is messy, definitions are unclear, and even extracting a single data point can require judgment. In bankruptcy, simple facts (i.e. cash on balance sheet, debt outstanding) can be disputed and depend on context or legal interpretation.

This talk explores what it takes to build AI for a complex, regulated, and judgment-heavy domain. I’ll share my start up (Axim's) approach to "analytical provenance" and "DistressedBench," a new eval framework designed specifically around the reasoning tasks required in distressed investing.

speakers.name: Harneet Kaur
speakers.bio: Harneet Kaur is the founder & CEO of Axim Intelligence, an early stage start-up building AI-native intelligence for distressed credit and restructuring. Before Axim, Harneet spent 10 years in finance, including at Morgan Stanley and as a distressed and special situations investor. She has a BS in Finance & Economics from NYU Stern and an MBA from the Wharton School.

sessions.title: Hunt before you're hunted: SonarQube Hunter Agent in action
sessions.description:
Attackers are starting to use autonomous reasoning to find and exploit vulnerabilities faster, while pattern-based scanners miss flaws that depend on intent rather than syntax. Hunter Agent is Sonar's guided reasoning agent, built to find the logic flaws conventional scanners can't see.
In this 15-minute live demo, watch it investigate a real application security scenario: connecting a SonarQube cloud project, running the security playbook, and tracing code paths and identity flows like a manual auditor. You'll see it catch broken access control, business logic flaws, and authentication or session vulnerabilities, then raise confirmed findings for your team to triage and fix.
You'll leave with a clear picture of how this adds an auditable, repeatable layer of security analysis to your existing workflow, helping teams catch deep logic flaws before attackers do.

speakers.name: Taylor Luttrell-Williams
speakers.bio: I'm a Dev Content Engineer at Sonar, where I leverage a background in full stack software development and DevOps, and a passion for teaching, to produce deep, technical content. I connect Sonar’s products to the global developer community, shaping how practitioners approach code quality and security, through hands-on educational content, such as technical tutorials, blogs, and videos.

sessions.title: Why Are We Still Governing AI Like Software?
sessions.description:
The biggest mistake we're making with AI agents is treating them like software.

Organizations have faced this problem before: how do you delegate real authority without giving up control?

in this talk, we will explore the Agent Accountability Framework and the agent governance principles taken from a century of human governance learnings.

sessions.title: Do Not Let Models Invent Numbers
sessions.description:
A human financial analyst would never put a number in front of a client that they cannot verify. Kepler has built an AI analyst that follows the same rule. It can only cite a figure that it has retrieved from a verifiable source.

That only works if search retrieves the right number. Vinoo will share how Kepler searches 100M+ SEC filings, earnings transcripts, and investor presentations across 14,000 public companies in one large shared namespace — alongside each client's private documents living in their own namespace — to return financial analysis generated from numbers that are never hallucinated.

You'll learn how to avoid analytical hallucinations by building an AI system that retrieves source material from very large indexes with high recall and low latency, a verification model that never allows a model to invent a number, and a security model that fully isolates privileged financial data.

speakers.name: Vinoo Ganesh
speakers.bio: Vinoo Ganesh is CEO of Kepler, the industry-agnostic, ground truth platform for AI, starting with finance. At Kepler, language models interpret financial questions and plan the analysis, while deterministic software retrieves source data, runs the calculations, and records how every result was produced. He started his career at Palantir, where he spent seven years working on the search and indexing backend, managing the Spark/YARN compute platform, leading customer engagements across the commercial, healthcare, and defense sectors, and running Project Frontline, Palantir's FDE rotation program. After Palantir he served as CTO of Veraset, a geospatial data startup that grew to $15M ARR before it was acquired, and before founding Kepler he was Head of Business Engineering at Citadel, overseeing data pipelines and investment platforms across the hedge fund. Kepler is backed by founders of OpenAI, Facebook, MotherDuck, dbt, Square, and others.

sessions.title: Beyond the Model Card: The Jagged Frontier of AI in Finance
sessions.description: Rayan Krishnan, CEO and co-founder of Vals AI, walks through what building industry-standard benchmarks has taught his team about the jagged frontier of AI in finance: the common failure modes, patterns of behavior, and why no single model leads on every task. No two workflows are identical, so independently evaluating models on your own work is essential for proving ROI, optimizing spend, and maintaining a competitive edge.

sessions.title: Why Frontier Models Fail on Billion Dollar Portfolios
sessions.description:
Your harness matters as much as your model when it comes to institutional buy-side research. In our benchmarks, moving one model to the right harness improved its score by more than 60%, as much as switching models entirely. Off-the-shelf agents fail because they miss hidden accounting traps, trust stale summary tables, and burn their token budget in degenerate search loops.

We’re launching Mandate-Bench, a benchmark built by LinqAlpha with Google DeepMind’s Kaggle Benchmarks team to test real investment origination: the work an analyst does before a portfolio manager ever sizes a position. We evaluate agents on licensed point-in-time market data across 1,300 US stocks and nearly 5,000 SEC filings, where only 15.8% of frontier model runs meet the bar of an institutional portfolio manager.

In this talk, we will walk through our benchmark findings and break down lessons learned from shipping agents in production to real hedge fund clients with billions in AUM.

speakers.name: Chanyeol Choi
speakers.bio: Chanyeol Choi is the Co-founder and CEO of LinqAlpha, a multi-agent AI platform for investment research used by leading buy-side and sell-side institutions globally. Chanyeol earned his Ph.D. from MIT and was named to Forbes 30 Under 30 in Science, North America. At LinqAlpha, he leads the team to build an LLM model-agnostic and data provider-agnostic architecture with institutional-grade security and governance. LinqAlpha's AI search engine, embedding model, recently ranked #1 on Hugging Face's MTEB leaderboard.

sessions.title: From Sharing Code to Sharing Agents
sessions.description: Delta is a futuristic agentic development GUI from the creators of the high-performance Zed code editor. This session demonstrates using Delta to work on a real-world problem, while explaining how Delta's CRDT-backed persistence system keeps a perfect history of not only code changes and conversation, but how the two relate. You'll also learn how it works asynchronously (or in realtime) with multiple human collaborators across multiple agents, and see a live demonstration of how this all comes together in practice on a real project.

sessions.title: Who is making the request? Agent Auth 101 via gateways + SDKs
sessions.description: An agent calls a tool, the tool calls an API, and every request has a valid credential. We'll examine how that flow can still give the wrong user access to a resource. Using a small MCP application, I'll trace a request through a gateway and an SDK-protected service, showing where user identity and delegated permissions need to travel. We'll compare the integration costs of both patterns and show how to combine them without rebuilding authorization in every application. The demo will use Keycard for credential exchange and policy-controlled access, then run allowed and denied cases against the protected flow. Attendees will leave with a practical way to decide where to enforce authorization, which identity context to preserve, and how to test access boundaries independently of the model's judgment.

sessions.title: How to build an AI code review agent: from the creators of Greptile
sessions.description:
Building a basic AI code review agent is easy. Building one that reliably catches meaningful bugs without overwhelming engineers with noisy comments is much harder.

In this session, Daksh Gupta, co-founder and CEO of Greptile, will explain how to build a production-quality AI code reviewer. He’ll cover five key improvements: better prompting and evaluation, using different models to write and review code, giving agents deep codebase and product context, testing changes inside live development environments, and routing each task to the most effective model.

Designed for teams building an internal reviewer or evaluating existing tools, this talk offers a practical look at the architecture, infrastructure, and tradeoffs behind AI code review at scale.

sessions.title: AI and the Future of Fundamental Investing
sessions.description: Jack Woodruff ran one of the largest books at Citadel and went on to found Candlestick Capital. Today he's the buyer every finance AI company wants to win, and in this fireside chat with Vinoo Ganesh, CEO of Kepler and former Head of Business Engineering at Citadel, he'll speak candidly about what AI is changing in fundamental investing and what it isn't. Jack will share where AI is saving real time in his process, what he'd never hand over to a model, and why the judgment call still belongs to the investor. They'll also take on the questions most people only ask in private. Will the biggest funds win everything? If everyone has the same models, where does alpha come from? And when does a number have to be right, not just plausible?

speakers.name: Jack Woodruff
speakers.bio: Jack Woodruff is the founder and former Chief Investment Officer of Candlestick Capital Management (CCM). Mr. Woodruff led the firm from its inception in 2019 through 2025, overseeing portfolio decisions and building CCM’s investment, research, and risk frameworks. Prior to founding Candlestick, Mr. Woodruff served as a Portfolio Manager in Citadel’s equity unit, Surveyor Capital, from 2010 to 2019, where he built and led an 18-person investment team and invested in more than 400 global equities across multiple sectors. Mr. Woodruff also worked at Sigma Capital, a division of SAC Capital Advisors, and previously held analyst roles at Northsound Capital and Trivium Capital. He began his career at Ernst & Young and maintains an inactive CPA license in California. Mr. Woodruff holds an MBA in Finance from the NYU Stern School of Business and a B.S. in Accounting from the University of Southern California. He currently serves on the University of Southern California Marshall Board of Leaders and Thrive Scholars New York Advisory Board. He also is a Senior Advisor to Connect Ventures and Kepler AI.

speakers.bio: Vinoo Ganesh is CEO of Kepler, the industry-agnostic, ground truth platform for AI, starting with finance. At Kepler, language models interpret financial questions and plan the analysis, while deterministic software retrieves source data, runs the calculations, and records how every result was produced. He started his career at Palantir, where he spent seven years working on the search and indexing backend, managing the Spark/YARN compute platform, leading customer engagements across the commercial, healthcare, and defense sectors, and running Project Frontline, Palantir's FDE rotation program. After Palantir he served as CTO of Veraset, a geospatial data startup that grew to $15M ARR before it was acquired, and before founding Kepler he was Head of Business Engineering at Citadel, overseeing data pipelines and investment platforms across the hedge fund. Kepler is backed by founders of OpenAI, Facebook, MotherDuck, dbt, Square, and others.

sessions.title: Your Agent Just Paid for Nothing (6 Attacks on x402 Payments)
sessions.description:
Agents can now discover paid APIs and authorize machine-to-machine payments without a human in the loop. Protocols like x402 make this work over plain HTTP. But a payment that settles correctly is not the same as a payment that should have happened.

I will walk through six attacks on an autonomous payment agent: price manipulation, duplicate payment, free shopping, payment-resource mismatch (the agent pays for one resource and receives another), malicious service discovery, and prompt injection into the payment decision. Two of them I will run live on a public testnet. In most, the transaction is technically valid, and still wrong: the agent overpays, pays twice, pays the wrong seller, or gets the wrong item. In one, the agent receives paid data with no payment at all.

Then the controls that actually constrain the surface, every one of them deterministic, with no model call in the authorization path: spending limits, recipient allowlists, resource binding, nonce checks, retry limits, and pre-payment validation.

Attendees leave with a threat model, a practical testing checklist, and a lab they can run against the official x402 SDK, on a testnet or a local simulation, without risking real funds.

Key Takeaways

• A working threat model for autonomous agent payments, with six demonstrated attack classes

• Deterministic controls that do not require another model in the loop

• A lab for testing your own x402 integration safely, on a testnet or a local simulation

• Why “the payment succeeded” and “the payment was correct” are different assertions

speakers.name: Ishween Kaur
speakers.bio: Ishween Kaur is a senior software engineer on Salesforce's AgentForce team, where she builds production agentic systems the harness, memory, guardrails and evaluation that keep agents reliable under real load and debugs them when they fail in ways a prompt can't explain. She is Communications Lead for Women in AI, and a seasoned speaker and workshop host who has run sessions across conferences and meetups over the past year. She showcases exact, working demos rather than hype and agent reliability.

sessions.title: Scaling AI with P&L on the line
sessions.description:
Optiver trades on thousands of instruments across every major exchange, and the code behind that has to be correct the first time. That's a demanding starting point for "AI-first." Over the past year we committed to it anyway: agents in every engineer's workflow, and a platform team whose job is to make the best way to build with AI also the easiest one.

 

This talk covers what that took, with the parts that didn't work included. We'll walk through the two-track operating model we settled on: a supported golden path with the tooling and guardrails engineers can rely on, and an experimental funnel where anything can be tried, on the condition that it emits telemetry and either graduates or gets sunset. We'll show why we stopped treating model choice as a vendor decision and started treating it as a market: task-specific exams as price discovery, a gateway that routes to the cheapest certified model, and independence built in through multiple channels and self-hosted open weights. And we'll get into the unglamorous parts, such as where inference spend actually goes once a few thousand people use agents daily (long-context work, not runaway sessions), why context-compaction savings mostly don't materialize, and how to keep cost controls from getting in the way of legitimate heavy work.

 

You'll leave with a concrete operating model, an evaluation approach that doubles as a routing signal, and a list of the assumptions we had to abandon.

sessions.title: State of the Agent: Reliability, Observability, and the Gap Between Them
sessions.description:
AI agents have moved from experiment to essential infrastructure. KPMG estimates agentic AI will drive $3 trillion in annual productivity gains, and a June 2026 industry survey found 57% of teams already have agents in production, but adoption has outpaced trust. The same survey found 32% cite quality as their top barrier, and Gartner projects more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by 2027 due to cost, unclear ROI, or inadequate risk controls.

That gap between "we built a demo" and "it survives production" is where most teams get stuck. Agents crash mid-task, lose progress, and fail silently in ways traditional monitoring never catches, and the more autonomous the agent, the more expensive that failure gets.

This talk is a status report were we'll talk about what's actually going wrong when agents hit production: the crashes, the silent failures, the debugging sessions nobody signed up for, and what the teams who've figured it out are doing differently. No single stack or vendor is the answer here; the point is the underlying shift in how you have to think about state, failure, and visibility once an agent is running unattended. You'll walk away with a framework for asking the right questions about your own systems, wherever you're building.

sessions.title: How to build financial agents that work across the web
sessions.description: Great financial agents unlock new ways to get work done across the web. Learn the core concepts behind browser-based agents, how to build them with Browserbase, and how companies like Ramp use them in production. You’ll leave with practical ideas for automating workflows across financial portals, from collecting receipts to retrieving documents.

sessions.title: Shipping like a startup, regulated like a bank
sessions.description: Inside Revolut’s internal coding stack with Together AI. Revolut became a fully licensed U.K bank in March 2026, and serves more than 75 million customers. Its engineering org still moves at startup speed. Holding both at once is the problem every engineer in financial services recognizes. Revolut runs two kinds of models against its internal coding work: Language models that turn written descriptions into working code, and vision models that turn mockups into a working interface. That second capability is the one most teams in fintech still haven’t shipped. You’ll leave knowing which of the two to deploy first, what changes when your codebase is subject to audit, and whether mockup-to-interface is ready for the work your team actually does.

speakers.name: David Abitbol
speakers.bio: David is a strategy consultant specialized in financial services, passionate about tech with a side hobby of statistical modelling.

sessions.title: Your agent fix just broke something else
sessions.description: Agent behavior emerges at runtime. So why are we still debugging only at the code level? A prompt edit, model swap, new skill, or tool change can fix exactly what you were looking at while quietly breaking something you weren't. In one example, a one-line policy fix raised an agent's action-safety score while dropping task completion from 0.89 to 0.72. The aggregate outcome looked fine. The regression was hiding underneath it. This session is a hands-on walkthrough of how to turn your agent observability into a continuous regression testing loop. We'll build a regression dataset from real production traces, run a candidate change against it as a full-agent experiment, diagnose competing metrics, and put the workflow into CI so every change is evaluated before it ships. We'll automate the full feedback loop from observe → evaluate → change → test → improve. Observability is becoming more than humans understanding agents. It's becoming the infrastructure agents need to understand and improve themselves.

sessions.title: Securing the Agentic Universe, One Layer at a Time
sessions.description:
Every enterprise is running agents that call tools, use MCP servers, and touch production systems, at volumes no human review loop can keep up with. That creates exposure: prompt injection, over-permissioned agents, MCP sprawl, and behavioral drift.

At enterprise scale, defense in depth is the only architecture that holds. No single control catches everything. You need policies, runtime threat detection, and fine-grained access controls applied at every layer of the agentic stack, paired with full-session observability and behavioral baselines so you can find signals in the noise.

You'll leave with a practical framework for securing AI agents without slowing adoption down.

sessions.title: From Model to Metrics: Serving and Benchmarking Any LLM Live with vLLM and Runpod
sessions.description: Choosing a vLLM version and serving config for a new model is usually guesswork and the wrong guess usually ships to production. In this live demo, we show vLLM BenchPod, Runpod's zero-setup template for serving and benchmarking any model on a single GPU pod. We boot a pod from a prebuilt image, serve a config, and watch vLLM come up with a live metrics dashboard. Then we run a real benchmark against the serving endpoint, swap configs, and compare results side by side, all with no repo checkout, no CI, and no infrastructure to manage. You'll leave with a working pattern for validating models and serving configs before they ever reach production.

speakers.name: Chris Vela
speakers.bio: Chris Vela is a Forward Deployed Engineer at Runpod. He has a vast experience helping clients scale their AI deployments on scalable GPU infrastructure. He has helped setup LLM and multi cluster deployments using Slurm and Ray. He also has a vast experience creating image diffusion models from creating backend APIs to model training. He has 10+ years of experience creating rapid prototype data solutions for the DoD, DARPA and startups. His solutions have been used for the Australian Army, the British Army and presented to the US Joint Artificial Intelligence Center and at the I/ITSEC 2019 Conference. He has experience creating data science solutions for transportation departments and social media analytics for a variety of Fortune 500 companies such as the NFL and Verizon.

sessions.title: Building Humanlike Voice Agents for Financial Services
sessions.description:
Financial voice agents operate in an environment where a misunderstood date, amount, identity, or authorization can become an operational and reputational risk. Yet teams often select models using component leaderboards and optimize latency metrics that do not reflect what callers actually experience.

 

This session examines voice agents as complete realtime systems rather than chatbots with speakers attached. Attendees will learn how speech recognition errors flow through an agent stack, why perceived latency differs from dashboard latency, how asynchronous tools preserve natural conversations, and how turn detection affects both user experience and task accuracy.

 

Using production examples and an open evaluation methodology, Jesse will show how to test complete conversations against real outcomes, including correct actions, privacy safeguards, efficient tool use, and natural turn-taking. Attendees will leave with a practical checklist for building and evaluating reliable voice agents in financial services.

sessions.title: Everyone Has AI. Who Has the Advantage?
sessions.description: Why do organizations with access to the same AI achieve vastly different results? This keynote explores the technical and organizational choices behind that gap - from choosing the right problems and redesigning workflows to building shared capabilities and feedback loops that turn AI into sustained competitive advantage.

speakers.name: Sid Pednekar
speakers.role: Head of Data and AI | Asset Management
speakers.bio:
Sid Pednekar, PhD, is a data, technology and AI executive who develops strategy and leads its execution. He builds capabilities that help organizations make better decisions, improve how they work and put new technology to practical use.

His work connects business priorities with technical and organizational choices: where to invest, what to build, how to allocate resources and what needs to change for a capability to succeed. He leads specialized teams and aligns business, technology, research and governance stakeholders around a shared direction. A recurring focus is turning bespoke solutions into reusable capabilities, supported by the ownership, workflows and adoption needed to make them effective across teams.

Sid’s experience is rooted in investment management, spanning quantitative research, alternative data, portfolio and risk analytics, and applied AI. Working closely with investment professionals has shaped his approach: understand the decision, identify where better information or a different process can help, and build around the people doing the work.

He holds a PhD in Computational Physics and Process Engineering. That scientific foundation informs how he approaches complex problems - reasoning from evidence, testing assumptions and understanding how the parts of a system interact. He brings the same discipline to strategy, team development and organizational change.

sessions.title: 2 years of shipping a production agent: what we rebuilt and what we kept
sessions.description: Arize started building its in-product agent on GPT-3.5 with a vision and no clear path. Two years and one full architectural rewrite later, it plans multi-step work, manages memory well past the context window, debugs itself from its own traces, and carries fixes through to pull requests. This talk is about the decisions along the way, especially the ones that got reversed. It covers why planning had to be built into the harness instead of left to the model, how the memory design changed once sessions outgrew the context window, what it took to use the agent to debug the agent without fooling ourselves, and what still needs a human in the loop after all of it. Every example comes from a real incident or a real design argument. Attendees building or maintaining a long-running agent leave with a list of decisions they'll face and a record of how one team made them.

sessions.title: Give the Model a Computer: The One Thing Every AI Agent Framework Agrees On
sessions.description:
Building an agent is easy. Deciding where its code runs is the part that follows you to production.

This talk comes from a year of building Daytona integrations across the agent ecosystem: LangChain, CrewAI, Google ADK, Mastra, Pydantic AI, the OpenAI Agents SDK, and a long tail behind them. Integration after integration, the same pattern kept surfacing. Frameworks that agree on nothing, not even the language, not the mental model, not who controls the flow, all converge on one identical primitive: give the model a computer. We'll trace why.

Every framework ends up facing the same question: where does the model's code actually run? Only three answers exist, and two of them stop holding once real users show up. That's why the past year went the way it did, with frameworks deleting their own code interpreters rather than defending defaults they couldn't. And that's why the computer keeps growing: first a tool call, then the place the agent lives, then a thousand machines at once.

You'll leave with one rule: pick the boundary before the framework. Frameworks are opinions. The boundary is a commitment.

sessions.title: AI in Production: Maintaining Quality and Trust as Output Scales
sessions.description: As AI agents take on more of the software development lifecycle, engineering teams face a new challenge: moving faster while maintaining code quality, consistency and control. This session explores how quality and governance can evolve alongside AI adoption, from shared coding standards to independent review and human oversight. Through practical examples and a live demo of Qodo, attendees will see how AI powered workflows can help teams scale development with greater confidence in the code they ship.

sessions.title: The Machine that Changed the World, vAI
sessions.description:
Software's future runs on agentic factories — and the same lessons that transformed manufacturing (prevent defects at the source, push quality control to the people doing the work, target the bottleneck) apply directly to building them. In a world of code abundance, the real constraint isn't model capability — it's verification: can you trust the code AI agents produce enough to put your name on it?

Tariq will show how enterprises can build software factories that ship fast and stand up to scrutiny, centered on three interlocking loops: an agentic loop that catches issues as code is generated, a CI verification loop that catches what slips through before shipping, and a maintenance loop that fixes issues already in production. Attendees leave with a practical framework for designing verification-powered agentic pipelines of their own.

sessions.title: Trusting Agents in Policy-Driven Workflows
sessions.description:
Institutional IT has run on one mantra for decades: People, Process, Technology. Agents now execute work that once required a human hand, and policy-controlled organizations need a model that accounts for them explicitly.

Using workflow examples and basic graph theory, we’ll show how to map a clear, auditable process while giving agents room to loop and go deep within defined boundaries.  We’ll also explore how software quality assurance changes when outputs are probabilistic.

Attendees will leave with a practical approach to deciding where agents belong, when humans should stay in control, and how to use measured quality to guide greater autonomy. The goal is to gain the efficiency of agents while preserving the controls, visibility, and accountability that policy-driven work requires.

speakers.name: Evan Kormos
speakers.bio:
Evan Kormos is an Engineering Manager at Coinbase, where he leads teams managing full stack delivery and service management.  Their focus is to bring AI agents into policy-governed automation in commercial Web3 products including Token Listings and the Coinbase Developer Platform. 

With a background in enterprise transformation, retail and commercial banking, and most recently with digital assets and AI, Evan brings a unique perspective on systems thinking and using software to maximize business value.

sessions.description: What does it take to turn advances in AI into meaningful progress for financial services? Joseph Kim, Head of ChatGPT for Financial Services, explores why and how the product was built, and the research and product direction guiding its evolution.
